transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in today?

Well... I guess I'm here because... man, I don't even know where to start. I've got this carpentry studio, right? Custom woodworking. I've been doing this since I got out of high school, working with my hands, building things from scratch. And I've always been a hard worker. I mean, twelve-hour days, breathing in sawdust, wrecking my back and my knees, just trying to keep the lights on and do good work. 

But... I came in today because I just hit this wall, and I honestly can't see this studio—or really my life, for that matter—ever getting back on track anymore. The bank, the suppliers, they keep calling and they keep putting these... these payment plans in front of me, telling me if I just sign this or restructure that, it'll be fine. But it's not fine. No matter how hard I work, no matter how many hours I put in at the shop, it's just pointless. I look around at my tools and my lumber and I just feel this heavy, crushing weight, like... like nothing is ever going to get better. It doesn't matter what I do or what paperwork they give me, it's all just a dead end now. Everything just feels completely broken, and I don't think I can fix it this time.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy, like your woodworking or other activities?

No, no, that's the thing. It's not that I don't care about the woodworking. I mean, if you put a piece of rough-sawn cherry in front of me right now, I'd still want to plane it down, you know? I still love the way the grain pops when you apply that first coat of Danish oil. It's... it's a beautiful thing. 

I've got this one piece in the shop right now, actually, a custom dining table. Live-edge walnut. And just the other day I spent maybe three, three and a half hours just hand-sanding the butterfly joints so they sit perfectly flush with the surface. Most guys, they'd just run a belt sander over it, maybe hit it with some 120-grit and call it a day, but I care about the details. I still care about making something that's going to last a hundred years, long after I'm gone. 

So, no, the passion for the actual wood, the building... that's still there. It hasn't gone anywhere. It's just... it's everything else around it that's suffocating me. The joy of the work just gets completely buried under the invoices and the supplier calls. Like, I'll be in the middle of routing a perfect edge, really in the zone, feeling good about how the bit is cutting and the smell of the sawdust, and then the phone rings. And it's the lumber yard asking about an overdue balance on a shipment of quarter-sawn white oak from two months ago. And suddenly the router just feels like it weighs a thousand pounds. 

But the interest in the craft itself? No, I haven't lost that at all. If anything, the wood is the only thing that makes sense to me anymore, even if the business part is completely ruined. I just... I wish I could just lock the doors and build, you know? Without all the noise. But you can't do that. You can't just ignore the bank. So I'm stuck loving this thing that's dragging me under.
Have you been feeling down or in a low mood most of the day, nearly every day, lately?

Yeah. Yeah, it's... it's like this heavy, gray feeling, you know? And it's not just lately, it's... it's most days. Honestly, almost every single day. I'll wake up—and I'm usually up early, like 5:00, 5:30, because that's when the shop is quietest and you can really hear the machinery run without the street noise—but before my feet even hit the floor, before I even put my boots on, I can feel it. It's just sitting on my chest. This... this weight. 

And I'll drag myself out of bed, make my coffee—black, same way I've drank it for twenty years—and I'll drive down to the studio. And like I said, I still love the wood. I really do. But even when I'm standing right there in the middle of it all, surrounded by these beautiful slabs of maple and ash and walnut that I used to just get so fired up to work on... it just feels so flat. Everything is just flat. 

I'll be standing there at the workbench with a chisel in my hand, ready to clean up a mortise, and I just... I have to fight with myself to actually make the cut. I have to fight not to just stand there, staring at the wall, staring at the sawdust on the floor. It's like I'm moving through molasses all day long. And it doesn't lift. It doesn't matter if the sun comes out, it doesn't matter if I get a good joint fitted perfectly. That gray, heavy feeling is just always there, humming in the background like a bad air compressor, just dragging me down, hour after hour, from the minute I wake up until I finally go back to sleep.
Have you noticed a significant drop in your energy levels or felt fatigued most days, even when you're not physically exhausted from work?

Yeah, man, it's... it's honestly beyond just being tired. I mean, look, I'm a carpenter. I'm forty-five years old, I've been doing this my whole adult life. I know what physical exhaustion feels like. I know exactly what it feels like to unload a whole flatbed of 8/4 rough-sawn oak by myself in the July heat. That's a good kind of tired, you know? Your muscles ache, but you earned it. 

But this... this isn't that. This is something else entirely. I'll get a full night's sleep, right? I'll actually be in bed for a solid eight hours, which I never used to do when the business was booming, but even after a full night in bed, I get to the shop and... I swear to you, by midmorning, my arms feel like I've been hauling lumber all day long. And I haven't even done anything heavy yet! I'll just be standing there at the bench, and I can barely push through the basic stuff. Just measuring out a piece of stock, or lining up a cut on the miter saw... it takes everything I have. 

And it's not even just the physical labor that does it. Even the small things, the office stuff. I'll sit down on my stool by the drafting table to return a couple of calls to clients or suppliers or whatever, and I just feel completely wiped out. Just dialing the phone feels like I'm trying to lift an anvil. I don't have the gas in the tank anymore. It doesn't make any sense because, like I said, I haven't even done the real work yet, but my body just feels totally drained, like my batteries are completely dead before the day even really gets going. I just sit there looking at my tape measure and thinking about how much effort it's going to take just to extend the blade. It's exhausting just existing right now.
Have you been feeling like you're failing or that you're not good enough, especially when it comes to handling the business side of things?

Yeah. Yeah, constantly. It’s... it’s honestly like a tape playing in my head on a loop these days. 

You know, it used to be that if I made a mistake—and everyone makes mistakes, even the old-timers who've been doing this for fifty years—you just... you grab another piece of stock, you reset your fence, and you start over. You learn from it. But now? Now it’s completely different. If I'm working on a piece and a joint doesn't line up perfect, or if I'm dealing with the office stuff and I miss a bid deadline because I just couldn't get the numbers together in time... I don't just look at it and think, "Okay, I messed up that cut," or "I dropped the ball on that paperwork." 

It goes straight to my gut. I start thinking I'm just a lousy carpenter. I look around at the shop, at the table saw, the planer, the thousands of dollars in tools and loans, and I just think... maybe I had no business trying to run my own studio in the first place. Who did I think I was? 

I should have just stayed a shop hand for somebody else, you know? Just punching a clock, sweeping up the sawdust at 5 PM, and letting someone else worry about the overhead and the clients. Because when you're the owner, every little failure is on you. And lately, it feels like I'm failing at all of it. Like, I missed a deadline for a custom cabinetry bid just last Tuesday. A big job, too. A kitchen remodel over in the Heights. The general contractor called me three times to get my numbers, and I just sat there on my stool, staring at the phone, feeling like a complete fraud. Like, if they actually knew how barely I'm holding it together, they wouldn't want me building a birdhouse, let alone a fifty-thousand-dollar kitchen. 

It just... it eats at you, doc. You start doubting every cut you make, every price you quote. You just feel like you're playing dress-up as a master carpenter, and everyone's about to find out you're a fake. Every little mistake just proves to me that I'm not good enough to be doing this.
Have you had any thoughts about not wanting to live anymore or that life isn't worth living?

No... no, doc, it's not like that. I mean, I know I just spent all that time telling you how miserable everything is, and how I feel like a total fraud drowning in my own sawdust most days, but... I don't want to die. I really don't. 

It's not about wanting to end my life, it's more like... I just want this *feeling* to stop. You know? Like, I'll be standing there looking at the bandsaw or the lathe, and I definitely think about just locking the deadbolt on the shop door, throwing a big blue tarp over the lumber racks, and just walking away from the business. Just selling off the inventory, auctioning the heavy machinery, and being done with the stress of it all. But walking away from *life*? No. 

I've got my family, and even though I feel like I'm letting them down by being such a mess lately, I could never do that to them. I remember when a buddy of mine, a guy I used to do some rough framing with back in my twenties—good guy, hard worker—when he passed away... it was a car accident, not suicide, but still... I saw what it did to his wife and his folks. It just completely hollowed them out. Left them as just shells of themselves. I'm not going to put my people through that. I could never intentionally leave that kind of mess behind for someone else to clean up. 

So, no, I don't sit there thinking about ending it. I don't have any thoughts of hurting myself or anything dark like that. I just... I'm just so tired of fighting this heavy feeling every single day. I want to wake up, walk into the shop, smell the cut pine, and actually enjoy it again, instead of feeling like I'm trapped inside a concrete box. I want to be able to look at a blueprint without my chest tightening up. But as far as not wanting to be here at all? No, I want to be here. I just don't want to be here feeling like *this*, if that makes any sense. I just want the old me back.
How long have you been feeling this way most days — the heavy, gray feeling you described — has it been going on for weeks, months, or longer?

Weeks? Months? Man, I wish it was just a few weeks. No, it's... it's been a lot longer than that. 

It started right around the time I took on the mortgage for the studio. That was a little over two years ago now... probably about two years and two months, if I'm doing the math right. I remember the exact timeline because it was supposed to be this massive milestone for me, right? I'd been renting space in other guys' shops for over fifteen years, always sharing the big tools, always fighting for bench space, always sweeping up someone else's mess. And then this place came up over on the east side—an old brick building, great bones, three-phase power already installed. It was perfect. 

So I went to the bank, I put together this whole crazy business plan, put everything I had on the line for it... the whole nine yards. And the day I signed that commercial mortgage, two years and two months ago, I really thought I was going to feel like I was on top of the world. Like I'd finally arrived, you know? But almost immediately... I mean, practically the very next day, this... this heavy, gray weight just settled right over me. 

I remember walking in there with the keys that first week, looking at the empty concrete floor where I was going to build my dream shop, and instead of being excited to start moving my heavy machinery in, I just felt this cold, miserable dread. And it just hasn't left me since. Every single day for over two years now, I wake up and I'm right back in that same gray fog. It’s like the ink wasn't even dry on those bank papers before the life just completely drained out of me. 

At first, I kept telling myself it was just the stress of the debt, you know? Just the reality of having a massive commercial loan hanging over my head. I figured, give it a few months, get some jobs under your belt, and it'll pass. But it never did. It's been twenty-six straight months of just... trudging through wet concrete. Every single day. I keep waiting to wake up and feel like the guy who was so hungry to open his own studio, but it's just been this endless, heavy slog ever since I signed that paperwork.
Have you had a depressed mood most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years?

Yeah, like I was just saying about the timeline, it's been over two years now, and it really is most of the day. Honestly, it's almost the entire day, more days than not. 

Most days I wake up, and before my feet even hit the floorboards, I've got this heavy, gray feeling already sitting right on my chest. Just... weighing me down before I've even had a chance to make a cup of coffee. I'll drag myself out of bed, get in the truck, and drive over to the studio. And you'd think getting to work would help, right? Because I've got all this beautiful lumber in there—walnut, cherry, some really nice quarter-sawn white oak that I paid a premium for. I used to just love working with that stuff. I used to run my hands over the rough grain and actually get excited about what kind of table or cabinet it was going to become. 

But now? I go in there, I'm completely surrounded by this wood I used to love, and it all just feels... flat. The whole world just feels flat and colorless. I'll be standing there in the middle of the shop, the heater going, the radio playing softly in the background, and I literally have to fight with myself not to just stand there staring at the wall. I'll just hold a piece of sandpaper or a tape measure, and I have to force my brain to actually do something with it, because otherwise I'd just stand there staring into space for hours. It takes everything I have just to make a single cut. And it’s like that from the minute I wake up until I finally go back to sleep. It just doesn't lift, doc. It never takes a day off.

And then this place came up over on the east side—an old brick building, great bones, three-phase power already installed. It was perfect. 

So I went to the bank, I put together this whole crazy business plan, put everything I had on the line for it... the whole nine yards. And the day I signed that commercial mortgage, two years and two months ago, I really thought I was going to feel like I was on top of the world. Like I'd finally arrived, you know? But almost immediately... I mean, practically the very next day, this... this heavy, gray weight just settled right over me. 

I remember walking in there with the keys that first week, looking at the empty concrete floor where I was going to build my dream shop, and instead of being excited to start moving my heavy machinery in, I just felt this cold, miserable dread. And it just hasn't left me since. Every single day for over two years now, I wake up and I'm right back in that same gray fog. It’s like the ink wasn't even dry on those bank papers before the life just completely drained out of me. 

At first, I kept telling myself it was just the stress of the debt, you know? Just the reality of having a massive commercial loan hanging over my head. I figured, give it a few months, get some jobs under your belt, and it'll pass. But it never did. It's been twenty-six straight months of just... trudging through wet concrete. Every single day. I keep waiting to wake up and feel like the guy who was so hungry to open his own studio, but it's just been this endless, heavy slog ever since I signed that paperwork.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a persistent low mood that meets the criteria for a major depressive episode lasting over two years, indicating a possible diagnosis of Persistent Depressive Disorder (F33.2) rather than Major Depressive Disorder (F32.2).
doctor.question: Have you had a depressed mood most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most days I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling already sitting on me, and even when I'm in the shop surrounded by wood I used to love, it all feels flat and I have to fight not to just stand there staring.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about experiencing a depressed mood most of the day, more days than not, which matches the Depressed_Mood symptom.

patient.answer:
Yeah, like I was just saying about the timeline, it's been over two years now, and it really is most of the day. Honestly, it's almost the entire day, more days than not. 

Most days I wake up, and before my feet even hit the floorboards, I've got this heavy, gray feeling already sitting right on my chest. Just... weighing me down before I've even had a chance to make a cup of coffee. I'll drag myself out of bed, get in the truck, and drive over to the studio. And you'd think getting to work would help, right? Because I've got all this beautiful lumber in there—walnut, cherry, some really nice quarter-sawn white oak that I paid a premium for. I used to just love working with that stuff. I used to run my hands over the rough grain and actually get excited about what kind of table or cabinet it was going to become. 

But now? I go in there, I'm completely surrounded by this wood I used to love, and it all just feels... flat. The whole world just feels flat and colorless. I'll be standing there in the middle of the shop, the heater going, the radio playing softly in the background, and I literally have to fight with myself not to just stand there staring at the wall. I'll just hold a piece of sandpaper or a tape measure, and I have to force my brain to actually do something with it, because otherwise I'd just stand there staring into space for hours. It takes everything I have just to make a single cut. And it’s like that from the minute I wake up until I finally go back to sleep. It just doesn't lift, doc. It never takes a day off.

inference.note: The patient has described a depressed mood occurring most of the day, nearly every day, for over two years, which meets the duration criterion for persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia). This rules out F32.2 (moderate depressive episode), as the duration is longer than what is typically considered for a major depressive episode and aligns more closely with chronic depression.
